initiative.title: Garden design app
initiative.summary: Desktop web app for Indiana homeowners: address and photos become an illustrated plan of the whole property; sun-aware AI designs; season and 5-year slider; a step-by-step planting and care plan.
initiative.next_action: Run spikes S1, S5, S15, S2, then the first proof.

sources.anchor: round 3: magic moment, output, control, device
round 4: plants, grid, sun, Indiana, time slider
round 5: themes, safety, overlap, annuals, sun orientation

claims.statement: Help people make landscaping decisions by storing property, plant, and goal data and turning it into visuals and simulations.

Start from photos (own library, phone, or listing photos the user saves) plus the address and a scaled aerial view; build a map of the whole property: house, driveway, fences, beds, trees. Close-enough accuracy.
Capture goals, budget, desired amount of change, and current satisfaction.

First user is a homeowner with a place for a garden: older, retired, and family people who open a URL; not Gen Z. Anne is the likely first real user. The first version is a product others can use, not only Anne's yard.
Professionals may get more value; making money is not a stated goal.
Must be highly visually appealing.
Gaussian splats from photos for 3D renders.
Understand time: seasons within a year and plant size out to about 5 years, especially trees. Monte Carlo weather runs are deferred.
A 2D landscape-architect plan view is the editing surface.
Deep knowledge of materials: paths, stonework, fence styles, and their interaction with planting.
Scenarios and long-term plans (trees over 5-10 years).
Maximize automation/AI: identify what exists, measure, suggest; user clicks through a gallery of proposals and mood-board elements.
Render styles: photoreal, artist (watercolor/isometric), playful game look; the game look is fun but likely not useful.
Garden explainer (e.g., Versailles over time) as a 3D historical tour.
Public portfolio for landscape architects.
Whole-property landscaping around the house is the target; planning a small area alone must also work and look good.
A person can start from a feeling or theme (peaceful, private, color), wildlife to attract, or safety needs (no thorns or toxic plants near kids and pets); the app turns it into plants and layout.
The app reviews the current yard: what looks good, what does not, and which spots are empty.
A reference photo of another garden can supply style elements to apply to the user property; the design stays anchored on the real property and borrowed ideas are labeled.
The magical moment is seeing your own house and yard appear from photos and the address.
Output: top-down plan (main), front view, current plus new plants and trees, and a step-by-step plan from now to the goal.
Beginners get 3 to 5 options, pick, and give feedback; experienced users give plants and ideas that act as constraints.
Used on a desktop computer at home; photos come by drag and drop; a phone only takes photos.
Visual plant gallery with filters for color and bloom time; drag plants onto the plan; every AI-placed plant can be moved, removed, replaced, or reworked by area.
Sun and shade are central and must be modeled per area of the yard.
Region, climate, and plants are limited to Indiana; start from about the top 100 Indiana plants.
Step-by-step plan covers planting windows, care schedule, time to grow, sun, soil, popular and easy choices, annual vs perennial, and yearly lift-and-replant work.
Time slider covers seasons within a year and extends to about 5 years.
The 2D plan is not a square grid: plants overlap and have real footprints. A 3D isometric view is wanted if it can be made beautiful; plant visuals need research.
Sun setup: address plus the direction the front door faces; show morning and afternoon shadows; user rotates until they look right; user can draw fence and property lines.
Plant data includes lifespan, annual vs perennial, replanting effort, and low-effort options including artificial plants.
Community use, such as the city of Fishers planning a peaceful public space, is a later direction enabled by being on the web.
Main look is a detailed watercolor illustration; each plant is painted with randomness so it looks organic; not photos.
Dragging a plant out paints an area of that plant.
A 3D pane beside the 2D plan updates at once with edits and the time slider, if it can be made fast enough.
Accounts with email and password only, simplest database; no magic links or private links; people must not lose work; sharing projects is important.
Later: simulate growth from seed to flower and plants that fill in or crowd out others.
Shared projects are view only.
Public gallery: owners mark projects public; a zoomed-out wall of thumbnails where you zoom in to see other gardens.

themes: AI proposals with full user control

shape.appetite: One property type (suburban Indiana lot), one region, about 100 plants. Enough to show Anne her whole yard. Not a platform.
shape.problem: Homeowners cannot picture a garden on their own yard, across seasons and years, or know what to plant where and when.
shape.recommended_shape: Accounts with email and password; aerial-first capture with AI-marked features and photos for appearance; watercolor 2D plan with per-plant variation as the editor; live 3D pane from the same data; AI picks plants and areas while code places, spaces, and checks sun; season and 5-year slider driving both panes; plan output; sharing.
success_moves: Measure from the aerial image and use photos for appearance; keep photo-to-3D reconstruction out of the first version.
Make beauty an illustration problem: watercolor plant art with seeded variation and one style guide, shared by the 2D plan and the 3D pane so the views always agree.
AI chooses plants, areas, and reasons; deterministic code does spacing, sun checks, and plant facts from a sourced data set.
Put each external service (aerial imagery, vision model, image generation) behind one narrow module with a saved-fixture version, so the prototype runs locally on one recorded property.
Every capture step has a manual fallback (draw outline, paint sun, place photos), so a failed AI step never blocks the flow.

first_proof.question: Can we turn a real Indiana address into a recognizable, beautiful illustrated plan, with 10 plants that change across 4 seasons and 5 years?
first_proof.artifact: Local web prototype for one real property: aerial base, AI-marked features with correction, 10 illustrated plants, time slider.
first_proof.decision_rule: If Byron and Anne recognize the yard after under 5 minutes of fixes and would show the plan to a friend, add the live 3D pane (S7), then designs and plan output. If the map fails, switch to guided drawing. If the art fails, finish S5 first.

rabbit_holes: Generalizing beyond Indiana or beyond suburban lots
Accounts and multi-device sync before the core view works
open_decisions: Proposed default: public gallery hides the address and aerial photo. Confirm.

history.event: Intent recovered from voice memo; brief drafted.
Five question rounds absorbed; intent brief rewritten; artifacts moved from planning task into the flower-power repo.
Shape brief and spike list written; first proof defined.
Round 6: watercolor look with variation, live two-pane 3D, email/password accounts with sharing. Shape and spikes updated.
Round 7: view-only sharing and a public gallery wall (S16).

questions.question: Who opens the app first?
questions.answer: Homeowner with a garden spot; older, retired, family people who use URLs. City use (Fishers) later.

questions.question: One spot or the whole yard?
questions.answer: Whole-house landscaping; a small area must also work.

questions.question: Design for a feeling?
questions.answer: Yes, plus wildlife themes, yard review, color themes, and reference images applied to my yard.

questions.question: Which moment must feel magical?
questions.answer: Photos in, your own house and yard appear; aerial view for scale; references clearly separate.

questions.question: What does a person leave with?
questions.answer: Top-down and front views, current plus new plants, step-by-step plan.

questions.question: How much does the app design?
questions.answer: Beginners pick from 3-5 options; experts give constraints.

questions.question: Where is it used?
questions.answer: Desktop at home; phone only for photos.

questions.question: How accurate must the map be?
What is in the step-by-step plan?
questions.answer: Planting windows, care, time to grow, sun, soil, popular and easy plants.

questions.question: Is the time slider in v1?
questions.answer: Yes: seasons in a year and out to about 5 years.

questions.question: Grid look or beautiful render?
questions.answer: Grid-like 2D is for editing but plants overlap, so not square cells; must be beautiful; 3D isometric if possible; plant visuals need research.

questions.question: Where does sun and shade data come from?
questions.answer: Address and front-door direction; show morning and afternoon shadows; user rotates until right; user draws fence and property lines.

questions.question: What should the main plan view look like?
questions.answer: Detailed watercolor illustration with randomness per plant so it feels organic; photos look repetitive. 3D after the 2D layout, ideally a live two-pane view synced with the slider.

questions.question: How do people save and return?
questions.answer: Accounts with email and password only, simplest database; sharing is important; no private links.

questions.question: Can a shared person edit?
questions.answer: View only for now. Also add a public gallery: mark projects public; zoomed-out small-multiples wall; zoom in to see a garden.
